text: Good to talk. What's the situation you want to think through? Give me the real version, not the tidy version.

Okay so this is a piece I have been thinking about, essentially reflecting on, like, I build all these tools for myself, right, the agents, the pipelines, the whole personal OS sort of thing, and I keep not publishing any of it. And there is this discourse, you know, build in public and all that, and I am doing amazing work I think, or good work, but it stays on my machine. So the question is something around, should I be packaging this as a portfolio, or is it more like, the work itself is the point, right, sort of. I don't know if that makes sense.

It makes sense, but I think you buried the real question. You're not asking about portfolio strategy. You're asking whether you're avoiding publishing because it's strategically correct or because you're afraid of what happens when people see your work.

Run a pre-mortem on this. Imagine it's six months from now and you still haven't published anything. What went wrong?

Yeah so the real version, okay. I want a better job basically, or better opportunities, like the AI PM sort of roles, or even founding engineer adjacent things. And my resume says PM things but the interesting stuff is all this building. So the portfolio is, it's coming from the question that, how does anyone even see this. But then every time I sit to publish I start perfecting, cleaning the repo, rewriting the readme, and then weeks pass and I ship nothing. Who am I even perfecting for, nobody is reading it yet.

That's honest. So the pre-mortem answer is clear: you'll have spent your energy on polishing instead of shipping, and the portfolio never exists.

This is a classic trap. You're optimizing for the wrong thing. You think the bottleneck is quality. I think the bottleneck is volume and consistency. A mediocre repo you published three months ago is worth infinitely more than a perfect one that lives on your machine.

So what's one piece of work you could ship this week, knowing it's not your best, and be okay with that?

The evidence, hmm. I mean, honestly the confidence is more like a feeling. A couple of founders I talked to got very interested when I showed the actual tools, like screen-shared, live. Nobody has ever asked me for a repo link. So maybe that is the evidence pointing the other way actually, that the demo is the asset, not the repo. But a public repo feels more, I don't know, legitimate, like proof it exists.

You just surfaced something useful. You have evidence that a live demo works on the people who matter. But you're ignoring that evidence because a public repo feels more legitimate.

That's a paper tiger. The fear that people need a pristine GitHub to take you seriously is probably not real. The people you want to impress are impressed by seeing the thing work.

So if you accept that the demo is the real asset, what changes about your next step?

My highest leverage hour right now is probably the practice tool itself, making it actually work for me daily. Publishing is the overhead dressed up as leverage. That is uncomfortable to say but I think it is true.

Now you're seeing it. Let me push one step deeper.

You said publishing is overhead dressed up as leverage. I think that's mostly true. But there's a smaller thing hiding inside it. The act of packaging something for others forces a clarity that building for yourself doesn't. You have to explain why it exists, what problem it solves, how it's different.

So my question is: is there a version of publishing that is leverage for your own thinking, not just overhead for other people's perception? And if so, what's the smallest version of that?

But then again, everyone senior I talk to has a blog or a repo trail, and hiring managers do google you, so maybe I am wrong and the polish does matter, maybe I should just spend the two weeks and do the proper public repo with the docs and everything. You probably think the demo thing is naive.

I don't think it's naive. I think you're ping-ponging between two strategies because both feel risky. Let me offer a way to resolve it.

Annie Duke calls this resulting — judging a decision by its outcome instead of its quality. You're doing the inverse: you're judging the strategy by how the outcome would feel, not by the probability it works.

So let me ask plainly: if you spent the next two weeks polishing the repo, and then nobody cared, would you regret the two weeks more than you'd regret shipping something rough and seeing what happens?

Your thinking was crisp on the pre-mortem and on recognizing that a live demo has better evidence behind it than a polished repo. You were honest about the paper tiger. Where it got vague was the ping-pong — you landed on a clear insight, then immediately second-guessed it by citing what senior people do, without testing whether that evidence applies to your specific situation.

One thing about how you talk: you said "everyone senior I talk to has a blog or a repo trail, and hiring managers do google you, so maybe I am wrong and the polish does matter." That sentence hedges three times — "everyone senior," "hiring managers do," "maybe I am wrong." You buried your own insight under other people's norms. Tighten it to: "I have evidence demos work. I'm choosing to ignore it because I'm scared of looking unpolished."

Exercise for next time: before you sit to publish anything, write a one-sentence strategy that your execution plan assumes. For example: "I get hired by demoing live tools, not by having a perfect GitHub." Then ask if your next action matches that sentence. If it doesn't, you're executing someone else's strategy.
